The puzzle club met on Thursday evenings in the community room above the Larch Street post office, and by October it had been working on the same puzzle for five weeks. It had fifteen hundred pieces. The picture on the box was a painting of a market square in the rain: striped awnings along the top, a crowd of umbrellas in the middle, and across the whole bottom third a wide gray puddle that reflected all of it.

Sela had joined in September, and she did the awnings. They were red and yellow and green, and a piece of awning could be placed in seconds. The puddle she left to Mr. Dabrowski, who had been coming to the club for eleven years and who worked on the gray every Thursday with the patience of a man filling out a tax form. He held each piece close to the lamp before he set it down. Once she asked how he could tell one gray from another, and he said that gray was mostly other colors, if you looked long enough.

She thought this was the kind of thing people said. But on the evenings when the awnings were finished and there was nothing left for her to do, she sat beside him and watched. After a while she began to see it too: a gray with a faint stripe of red in it, from an awning upside down in the water; a gray with a curve of black at one corner, the reflected edge of an umbrella.

On the first Thursday of November the puzzle was complete except for one hole, a little left of center, in the puddle. The four of them searched the floor, the chair cushions, and their own sleeves. Mrs. Ito turned the box upside down and shook it. Mr. Ito said the company would mail a replacement piece if they wrote, though it might take a month. Mr. Dabrowski said nothing. He sat with his hands folded, looking at the hole.

Sela looked down the table. Earlier that evening Mrs. Ito had opened the next puzzle, a harbor at dusk, at the far end of it to count the pieces, and had then swept them back into the lid with the side of her hand. The lid now sat on the shelf by the door. Sela went over and stirred the heap with one finger. Most of the pieces were the dark blue of evening water. One was gray, with a thin red line along one edge.

She carried it back between two fingers and pressed it into the hole. It fit.

Mrs. Ito clapped. Mr. Dabrowski looked at the piece for a long moment, and then at Sela. Then he went to the shelf, brought back the harbor lid with its heap of pieces, and set it down in front of her.

"The water's yours this time," he said.

Sela tipped a handful of dark pieces out under the lamp. She began to sort them, not by color, exactly, but by what was in the color.

When I was small I thought it called them in,
the white tower on the point at Gannet Head,
sweeping its one long arm across the water
the way my father waved us in for supper.

Every eleven seconds, the beam.
I counted it from the back seat of the car,
from the porch, from the bunk at my aunt's cottage,
and each time it came around I felt chosen.

It was my aunt who told me what it meant.
She had grown up two houses from the cliff,
and she said a lighthouse is a sign that reads
stay back, in a language every boat can read.

I had it backward, then, the whole time:
the light was the one thing on that coast
that wanted nobody to come near it,
and said so, plainly, every eleven seconds.

Under the point the ledges run out half a mile,
black rock a few feet below the surface,
and the light is there to say so, all night,
to every hull that comes close enough to wonder.

So the beam that crossed my bedroom wall
was meant for someone else: a stranger
miles out in the dark, who would see it once,
and turn the wheel, and go on home to supper.

I go back some summers. It runs by itself now,
a lamp on a timer, the keeper's house a gift shop
selling postcards of the thing it does.
People lean on the railing and photograph it.

I stand among them, still counting to eleven,
and think of the boats I will never see
that caught it once, far out, and swung away,
which is all it ever asked of them, and enough.

The summer I was twelve, my cousin Rafi had a newspaper route of forty-one houses on the streets behind the high school, and in the second week of July he went to a soccer camp two hours north and left the route to me. He was fifteen and had carried it for two years. The night before he left, he wrote it out for me on a sheet of lined paper: street names, house numbers, and arrows showing which way to turn at each corner.

I was out the door at half past five the next morning with the canvas bag over my shoulder, and I was finished by a quarter to seven. I remember being pleased with the time. I had folded each paper in thirds the way Rafi had shown me and thrown it, mostly accurately, onto each porch on the list.

By noon my aunt, Rafi's mother, had taken four phone calls. Mrs. Varga on Hollis Street wanted her paper inside the storm door, because the wind took it. Mr. Bell's went on the left side of his step, the side away from the railing he used. The family at 18 Crane Street had a dog that ate newspapers, and their paper went in the mailbox. The man at the end of Lowell Road paid extra to have his before six, because he read it on the early train.

None of this was on the sheet. That evening I called Rafi at camp, and he went through all forty-one houses from memory, without a pause, while I wrote. The woman at 9 Hollis liked her paper rolled instead of folded. The Brennans were away until the twentieth. Mr. Bell sometimes waited on the porch, and if he did, you handed the paper to him and asked about his tomatoes.

"Why didn't you write any of this down?" I asked. He seemed puzzled by the question. "I just know it," he said.

For the rest of the week I carried two sheets. One was his list of streets. The other was mine, three pages long by Friday, with a line for every house: storm door, left side, mailbox, before six, ask about tomatoes. I was slower than on the first morning, sometimes by half an hour, and the phone at my aunt's house stayed quiet.

Mr. Bell was on his porch on Thursday. I handed him the paper and asked about his tomatoes, and he told me about them for ten minutes, until I had to run the last stretch to make Lowell Road by six.

When Rafi came home I gave him both sheets. He read mine through, standing in the driveway with his duffel bag still on his shoulder, and then he folded it in thirds, like a newspaper, and put it in his pocket. I had thought the route was forty-one houses. It turned out to be forty-one people, and he had been carrying all of them in his head.

item.passage:
Ask a teacher how long an assignment should take and you will usually get a reasonable answer: twenty minutes, maybe thirty. Ask a ninth grader how long last night's homework took and you may get a very different number. Both can be telling the truth. Each teacher sees one assignment. The student sees five of them, stacked on the same kitchen table, after practice and dinner.

This is why I have come to think that homework should be given a nightly time limit, set by the school and stated in minutes rather than in pages. A rule of that kind sounds like a gift to students who would rather be doing something else. It is really a tool for teachers.

Consider how homework is usually planned. A teacher chooses twenty problems because twenty seems about right, and the cost of that choice, an hour or an evening, is paid by someone else, at home, out of sight. Almost every other demand in a school day has a visible price. A class period ends when the bell rings. A test fits the time printed on it. Homework alone is measured by the task, and the task does not know what time it is.

A limit changes the question a teacher has to ask. It is no longer "What should they practice?" but "What is worth forty minutes of their evening?" That is a harder question, and a better one. Shortened homework tends to be chosen homework: the five problems that reveal whether a student understands, in place of the fifteen that merely repeat them.

The first objection is that some students need more time, and some want it. A student preparing for a competition, or one who has fallen behind and is catching up, may sit at the desk long after any limit has run out. A limit should bind the assignment, though, and leave the student free. Its job is to tell the school how much it may ask for, and a student who chooses to do more is answering a different question.

There is a second objection, that students will learn to watch the clock rather than the work. Some will. But students already watch the clock; they simply have no idea, at eight o'clock, whether the night will end at nine or at eleven. A known limit lets them plan, and planning is itself one of the things homework is supposed to teach.

A school day is a list of promises about time. Homework is the one place where the school has so far declined to make one.

In the 1880s nearly every load of hay sold in Kesslerton went across the town scale on its way to market. The scale stood at the north end of the square: a wooden platform big enough for a wagon and team, laid over a brick-lined pit, with a shed beside it where the weighmaster read the iron beam and wrote out a ticket. Buyers paid by the ticket. A farmer who wanted to know what his season was worth learned it there, a wagon at a time.

In the summer of 1884 the farmers began to say that the scale weighed light. Their loads came out a hundred pounds or more under what experience told them a wagon held, and a hundred pounds of hay was real money. Suspicion settled quickly on the weighmaster, Amos Pruett, whose brother-in-law bought hay for the livery stable. Pruett offered to let any farmer stand in the shed and read the beam alongside him. It changed few minds.

In September, at Pruett's own request, the council sent for the county sealer of weights and measures, a man named Josiah Wend, who arrived with a wagon of cast-iron test weights, each stamped fifty pounds. With a crowd watching, Wend's helpers stacked twenty of them, a thousand pounds, on the platform. Pruett read the beam aloud: nine hundred and ten.

Several of the farmers present took this as the end of the matter. Wend did not. He lit a lantern, lifted the trapdoor at the corner of the platform, and climbed down into the pit. The spring floods, he found, had washed a bank of silt under the north edge, and it had dried there as hard as brick. When a heavy load pressed the platform down, one corner came to rest on that ridge of mud, and part of the weight went into the ground instead of into the levers that moved the beam. The heavier the load, the more of it the mud took.

Two men spent a day clearing the pit with shovels and buckets. When the test weights went back on, the beam read one thousand.

Pruett kept his post for another nineteen years. The first thing he asked of the council afterward was money for twenty fifty-pound weights of the town's own, to be kept in the shed, so that any farmer who doubted a reading could test the scale on the spot. The council also ordered the pit cleaned every April. Pruett, asked years later what the trouble had taught him, said that he had always been willing to be watched. What the scale had lacked was a way to be checked.

item.passage:
Anyone who spends a few days at the seashore notices that the water keeps a schedule. Twice a day, on most coasts, the sea creeps up the beach and then slides back, and each day the high water arrives roughly fifty minutes later than it did the day before. That delay is the first clue to what drives the tides. Fifty minutes is also about how much later the Moon rises each day.

The Moon pulls on everything on Earth, but it does not pull on everything equally. Gravity weakens with distance, so the ocean on the side of Earth facing the Moon is tugged a little harder than the planet's center, and the center is tugged a little harder than the ocean on the far side. The result is a stretching. The water nearest the Moon is drawn slightly toward it, and the water on the far side is, in effect, left behind. The oceans bulge outward in two places at once: one under the Moon and one directly opposite.

Earth turns beneath these two bulges once a day, and a given stretch of coast passes through both of them. That is why most shores get two high tides a day rather than one. Because the Moon moves along its orbit while Earth turns, a coast needs a little more than a full day, about twenty-four hours and fifty minutes, to return to the same position beneath it, which accounts for the daily delay.

The Sun raises tides too, by the same stretching effect. It is vastly more massive than the Moon but also far more distant, and the stretching depends strongly on distance, so the Sun's tidal effect is a little less than half the Moon's. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up, at new moon and full moon, the two effects add together, and high tides run higher and low tides lower than usual. These are called spring tides, a name usually traced to the idea of water springing up; it has nothing to do with the season. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, near the quarter moons, the range shrinks, and these are called neap tides.

The two-bulge picture explains the rhythm of the tides, but it cannot explain their size. In the open ocean the rise and fall is modest, often about a meter or less. In the Bay of Fundy, between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, the difference between high and low water can exceed fifteen meters. The continents make the difference. They block the bulges from sweeping freely around the globe, so the water in each ocean basin sloshes back and forth in huge, slow waves, and the shape of a bay can build up that motion, the way a push timed just right sends a swing higher. Some coasts, oddly, get only one high tide a day, and there are points at sea where the tide barely rises at all.

So the tide on any particular beach is the product of two things: a simple rhythm set in the sky, and a complicated answer given by the shape of the land and the sea floor. The Moon keeps the time. The coast decides how loudly the hour is struck.
